1.	As a result of reconnaissances and investigations made with regard to navigation in the Hudson bay is it possible to give an estimate of the period during which navigation is open?
2.	During what months is navigation ordinarily open in the Hudson bay with access to Fort Churchill and Port Nelson?

With respect to the probable length of the navigation season through Hudson bay and strait, no conclusive data is as yet available. During the last three seasons the river at Churchill has opened and closed on the fol-

Questions
lowing dates: 1927: June 20-November 3; 1928: June 19-October 11; 1929: June 20- November 2.
This does not mean that the route would be completely available between those dates, as ice frequently remains off shore for several weeks after the opening of the river. Neither does it mean that the route would not be available to a later date by the use of icebreakers to be provided.
The Hudson strait expedition, of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, reported that vessels passed through the strait inbound on July 19, 1927, and July 21, 1928, and that ice commenced to form at Nottingham island on November 16, 1927, in which year there were 120 dtays, or practically four months, during which commercial vessels could have navigated with safety without the assistance of ice-breakers. The report points out that the observation of two seasons only is scarcely sufficient on which to base any accurate statement in regard to the opening, closing, or length of the season of navigation. The length of season will probably vary considerably from year to year, and what effect on the extension of the season may be exerted by the use of ice-breakers at both Churchill and Nottingham island, where ice first forms in the strait, remains to be demonstrated by actual experience on the opening of the route.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED REDUCTION TO CORRESPOND WITH RATES ON AGRICULTURAL MACHINERY
speechtext:
Whereas motor trucks are now largely used in place of wagons for hauling grain and other produce to primary markets, therefore be it resolved that, in the opinion of this house, the customs tariff on motor trucks should be reduced to a level corresponding to that charged on other agricultural machinery.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, I have not chosen
this item in the customs tariff simply because it is the only one that could be attacked. I have chosen it because I have come to the conclusion that the farmers of this country must have cheaper motor trucks made available to them, and because I believe that the manufacturers of motor trucks have established their financial position in a way which demonstrates that this reduction might very well be made.
I think this resolution can be supported by hon. gentlemen in all quarters of this house. I would point out that it is very closely in line with a resolution which was moved by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen in 1911, namely:
That in the opinion of this house, a substantial reduction in the import duties on agricultural implements is now due the agriculturists of Canada, and is in just accord with the true ends of a protective tariff.
In his speech on that occasion Mr. Meighen pointed out that it had been one of the guiding principles of the national policy-which I may say has been in effect for the last fifty years, regardless of which party was in power -that as industrial concerns developed and secured a good hold of the home market as 
well as the export market, these duties should be diminished or in some cases wiped out altogether.
Now, may I quote very briefly from Mr. Meighen's argument on that occasion. He said:
It is this, that im .their attempts to continue the national policy-
He was referring then to the Liberal party which was in power.
-which had obtained for years bp-fore, they have overlooked, they have neglected one essential feature of that policy, they have quite forgotten its guiding principle, namely, the principle that as our industrial institutions advanced in strength and as they were able with every advance to acquire a hold on the home market, the import duties were to be diminished and adjusted in order to meet the evolving and changing conditions. It is that restraining, guiding principle which I claim this government has entirely overlooked, and as a consequence they have allowed, in the respect which I am discussing this afternoon, protection to run rampant, and they have for reasons that are only too obvious, become the slaves of those who helped them into power and who now maintain them there behind ramparts of gold.
Then I might quote further from Mr. Meighen's speech where he cited the remarks made by the late Hon. John Haggart:
For the last fourteen years, protection in Canada has so developed our manufactures that the government now think that a fair reduction in 'the tariff be ventured on.
That is by a Conservative finance minister-
They believe that our people can compete with less proteetioin than 'formerly, and to prove that, it can 'be pointed out that we are now sending agricultural implements to many portions of the world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I think this industry, judged by their ability to export their products, certainly could stand some reduction of the 20 per cent duty which they enjoy today. These are the export figures for motor trucks for the last few years

This is the opinion of Mr. Henry Ford himself, as reported in the Automotive Daily News of Detroit, under date of April 28, 1926, and as reprinted in report no. 3 on automobiles of the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation.
"I believe in free trade everywhere" says Henry Ford in the Detroit Times. "The tariff
is a hmdrarace to trade. Free competition brings healthy business."	_	_
Ford's statement was made in connection with the Canadian tariff reduction on mostor cars, and after visiting the plants of the Ford Motor Company of Canada. "Those fellows over in our Canadian unit," said Mr. Ford, "are going to manufacture more efficiently now. They'll have to. It's going to he a better plant over there-better organization. That's another reason why it's a good thing for the manufacturer.
They've been able to get a higher price in Canada, and naturally they've taken it. But on the other hand lower prices mean more buyers, more buyers mean more business, more business means more growth for the manufacturer. Give me that pliant at Ford city and IT; compete with the plant here at Highland Park any day. Our unit in Canada cam buy as cheaply as we can here. We make every part of the car in the Canadian plant, and 95 per cent anyway of the raw material is supplied right in Canada.
It was suggested that large scale productions make a difference, as many Canadian manufacturers believe they cannot compete with American manufacturers because the latter have advantages in mass production.
"I don't see that," said Mr. Ford. "What do you mean by mass production? I think we've got large scale production in our Canadian unit. They're turning out 600 cars a day. Here vve are doing between 7,000 and 8,000 a day, but I don't think that's any advantage after a certain -point."
Mr. Ford is the most outstanding man in the motor industry to-day, and I think his opinion in this matter should carry a great deal of weight with this house and, I hope, with the finance minister.
I never could understand, Mr. Speaker, why any national policy should allow a manufacturer to charge a Canadian more for his product than is charged outsiders, or, to .put it another way, a policy under which we sell a motor truck to our competitors in the Argentine, for instance, at a lower price than we sell bo our own producers.

The price at Edmonton of this truck chassis is $836.75 and at Boise, Idaho, which the board

In passing I would draw the attention of this house to the fact that this truck costs $8.60 more at Edmonton than at Victoria, British Columbia, although Victoria is 700 or 800 miles more distant. The price of this Ford truck chassis at Halifax is $748.75, while the price at Boston, which is approximately the same distance, is $586.40, or a difference of $162.35. May I repeat that the difference in price at the factory is $136.75, which leaves an added difference of about $26 in the maritime provinces as compared with Ontario.
The other point I wish to make is brought out in the report of the tariff board hearing. Ip 1926 the late Minister of Finance removed the excise tax on cars produced in Canada costing less than $1300 provided that 50 per cent of the car was produced here. The understanding of this house, the understanding,
I am sure the minister had, and the information he gave this house was that the manufacturers would not take advantage of this reduction in setting the prices of their cars in Canada. This matter was referred to the tariff board, and in passing I should like to point out some evidence in regard to it. The chairman was examining Mr. Russell in regard to this very point. He said:

There is another matter to which I should like to refer if I have time; I think this is brought out clearly in the memorandum submitted by the Ford Motor Company to the tariff board. It refers to the amendment to the Customs Tariff in 1926, which granted a 25 per cent drawback on materials imported and used in cars 50 per cent produced in Canada. The Ford Motor Company say in regard to this:
We wish to draw attention .to the fact that the original act required a Canadian content of 50 per cent to qualify for home consumption drawback and likewise to qualify the lower

Tariff on Motor Trucks-Mr. Coote
priced cars for exemption from excise tax. The wording of the act requires that individual models be qualified.
A supplementary regulation issued by the Department of National Revenue (not authenticated by legislation or order in council) permitted qualification for home consumption drawback (but did not provide for exemption from excise tax) on the basis of total factory output of all models, provided that 50 per cent of the total cost of production was incurred in Canada; provided also that each individual model has at least 40 per cent Canadian content, or alternatively, that certain production operations, such as chassis assembly and body trimming and finishing have been performed in Canada.
The obvious result of the application of the departmental ruling is that in qualifying a factory output, any excess Canadian content in one particular car or line of cars, allows just bare assembling of chassis and body trimming and finishing to be performed on the other cars produced, thereby obtaining drawback and possibly escaping payment of excise tax, contrary to the provisions of the act.
It seems to me that these manufacturers who were able to go to the commisisoner of customs and get him to issue such a regulation certainly are able to take care of themselves in almost any situation. I think before the session is ended this matter should be thoroughly discussed and some explanation furnished as to the authority of the commissioner of customs to issue regulations which in the opinion of some of the men appearing before the tariff board and some of the manufacturers is really a variation of the act itself.
The agriculturaf producers of Canada are placed in a difficult position. They are facing world competition and a great deal of the grain produced has to be hauled twenty to thirty miles. In some of the outlying districts, such as the Peace River district, some of the grain is hauled eighty miles to the railway point. These men are forced to use trucks. In many districts the hauling of grain in wagons is just as obsolete as the wearing of petticoats is said to be. The introduction of the grain combine harvester has necessitated the use of motor trucks, and the present condition of the wheat market should convince even the most optimistic of our friends that we are facing very keen competition and, our production costs must be reduced to the very minimum. I do not think I need to labour that point.
During 1928 the number of trucks and commercial cars in use in the three prairie provinces increased by over 10,000, and I think it is fair to estimate the increased cost of those trucks due to the tariff at $200 per truck. A short time ago I gave the increased cost of trucks, but that only covered the

The duty on agricultural machinery has been reduced at various times by different governments until it stands at 10 per cent or lower for the general tariff on the majority of agricultural implements. Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance):	Mr. Speaker, I thought that
probably we might expect to hear from a number of the members regarding a resolution

which would be of a very far-reaching character if adopted by the house. However, I am not raising that point as I presume an expression of the views of the house is sought on the basis of the evidence presented, rather than a decision by the house on a matter of fiscal policy which can be made only by a resolution presented through the medium of the committee of ways and means, made at the proper time and in the proper place. Therefore, I cannot pretend to indicate to-day what proposals may or may not be brought down in the budget as they would bear upon this or any other matter; all I can say is that I hope there will be a very full discussion and that every member taking part will endeavour to contribute something by way of information. As my hon. friends are well aware, each fiscal proposal which comes down in the budget must be presented to the committee of ways and means by way of a separate resolution dealing with itself. That has 'been the established practice of dealing with budgets through a great number of years, not only in Canada -but in all British parliaments, and personally I doubt very much whether the discussion of resolutions of this character, .framed exactly as this one is, is really in order. I do not, however, raise 'that objection, because I have not had time to investigate the bearing of it.
I call attention, however, to the difference in wording between this resolution and the one next immediately following which reads:
In the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of-
The sponsor of it worded it in this way because he recognized that such a proposal as he is there advocating, must, if it is to become effective, emanate from the government, and in the meantime the house is asked to express its opinion that the government should take into consideration the advisability of the course proposed. That is all I have to say on the subject, except to request that hon. members who give information particularly dealing with matters where figures and statistics have such an important bearing on the case, should take every care to present exact figures and facts with regard to the matters under discussion. That after all, is the primary reason for the establishment of the Advisory Board on Tariff and Taxation. I a;m not afraid of the facts if we are sure we have the facts before us on any particular question.

speechtext:
I
had expected my hon. friends to the right would have risen in somewhat righteous in-[Mr. Dunning.!
dignation against this resolution. I had in mind the pilgrimage of 1926 and I expected to hear in front of the parliament buildings the tramp of some three or four thousand men from Oshawa objecting to the reduction in the tariff to the ruination of the automobile industry. I did not, however, hear this, and as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has asked for some facts bearing upon the case, I can give him some. I have a few facts in connection with the reduction that was made in the duties on automobiles in 1926. If the reduction in the automobile duties in 1926 produced certain effects, it is reasonable to suppose and to argue that like causes will produce like effects. In 1926, after the celebrated pilgrimage and the protests of ruination were made, the dealers themselves had something to say about the matter, not simply as a political affair, but to their own particular agents, and I propose to read just two letters which were written by the Chevrolet motor people to the'ir agents in connection with the actual reduction in the automobile duties at that particular time. Immediately after the reduction in the duties, they wrote this letter to their agents:
Owing to existing conditions caused by the tariff reduction proposals

Irrespective of whether there was any excise reduction or not.
-on finished ears in the recent budget, the following mew retail delivery prices will apply for Chevrolet ears.
Then there follows a list of cars with the different prices. A car that was formerly priced at $90S was then priced to retail at $844, making a saving of $64 to the man who bought it. In fact, I knew at that particular time one man who entered a Chevrolet agent's office and asked him the price of that particular car. When the dealer quoted him he said that he could not afford it then, so he left the garage and went home. Two weeks afterwards he came in again and the same oar was standing there. He asked what the present price of the oar was, and the agent told him it was reduced $64 on account of the reduction made in the duty on automobiles. One would have a very hard time to convince that man, at any rate, that the reduction in the price of that car was not caused by the reduction in the tariff. Another car which was formerly priced at $1,165 was reduced to $1,058, or a reduction of $107. Another high-priced car which was formerly quoted at $1,262 was then priced at $1,178, also showing a reduction in price. One would have a very hard time to convince any of those men that the

Tariff on Motor Trucks-Mr. Ross (Moose Jaw)
reduction, in price was not due to the reduction in the tariff, because the company itself had said so.
What effect did that have upon the business? Did it retard the business? Did the business go to ruin on account of it? Let us see. Orders were sent in immediately after the reduction in the tariff, and about a month later this same retail dealer of Chevrolet cars received this letter which I wish to put upon Hansard:
We received yours of 'the 28th ult. in connection with your order for carload of Chevrolet cars.	,
Beg to advise that we are doing everything in our power to hurry along your Shipment of cars but so far have not been successful, although expect same will be shipped any day. We appreciate very much that our dealers are losing a certain amount of business this year but you are no douibt aware our factory is operating at capacity at the present time and during the past few weeks we have not been able to keep up with our orders, however, we hope 'that within the next week or ten days to get entirely caught up with our shipments and you may rest ,assured we will do everything in our power to rush this load along to you.
Evidently the lower price of the car increased the sales because it increased the farmer's purchasing power. I think the minister might well take this evidence, not from a politician, but from the dealers, and expect like causes to produce like effects. I think that a decrease in the duties on motor trucks, and consequently a decrease in the price, would increase the sales, and not hurt in any way either the manufacturers or the dealers. On the contrary, more cars will be made, and more cars sold, and there will be more employment for our workingmen, which I am sure my friends to my right desire as I do myself.

speechtext:
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has asked the different members of the house to express their views Upon this resolution. If we go back to the sessions of 1925-26 and 1926-27, it will be remembered that the opinion then expressed on this side of the house, as well as in the corner where the mover of the resolution (Mr. Coote) sits, was that a reduction in the tariff on automobiles would increase the sales, would lower the price, and would give greater employment throughout the Dominion. All these things have come true just as we predicted, and I am glad to see that my friends the Conservatives have learned a much needed lesson and that they are now saying nothing against a resolution of this kind at this time, although
they fought tooth and nail in the sessions of 1925-26 and 1926-27 against a reduction in the tariff on automobiles.
I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that we need to-day to present figures in regard to automobiles and trucks, because we have had practical proof of the benefits of a reduction in the tariff on automobiles, and those benefits have extended to everyone in Canada.
My hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) is moving for a reduction in the tariff on motor trucks. He believes, as I do, that a reduction in the tariff on motor trucks will lower the price of the motor truck to users in Canada, and as the farmer in western Canada is very much interested in a lowering of the price of his machinery of production, I am in favour of this resolution.
We have in Canada to-day a peculiar situation in regard to our grain. A few years ago men who had lived for many years in western Canada were advocating that the farms of western Canada be split up from whole sections, three quarter-sections and half-sections, into quarter-sections. Men who have noted the trend in western Canada realize that there has been a vast change, and that instead of the farms in western Canada becoming smaller and smaller they are to-day growing larger on account of the modern machinery that is being used on the farm. The tractor is now beyond the experimental stage and is being used night and day on the farms of western Canada. The combine harvester, another new machine in the last few years, is also being used extensively, and along with the combine harvester, the motor truck for the transportation of grain to the elevator is almost a necessity in western Canada to-day. I have followed with a great deal of interest the addresses on this resolution. I very frequently find myself in accord with the views of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), and I do in this particular matter. The farmers in all parts of the world find themselves in distress to-day, and in the United States great efforts are being made to relieve the farmers from the difficulties in which they now find themselves. The same is true of other countries. I was talking recently to a man who travelled last summer in Denmark, that little country that is supposed to be the most advanced in farming of all countries of the world, and he said that it was surprising the number of people who made inquiries about Canada with a view to settling here. The farmers of western Canada in their production of grain find themselves at a very great disadvantage as compared with other grain growing countries, and particularly wheat growing countries, because we are far from tide water, whereas in the Argentine, Australia and other countries the grain fields are close to tide water or to navigable rivers. That gives them a very great advantage.
Again, in recent years, plant diseases have increased to a very great extent. Rust twenty years ago was almost unknown in this country; at least, damage from rust was almost negligible. To-day rust is a very great menace to the wheat grower of western Canada. I think it is only fair and right in the interests of all Canada that the implements of production should be reduced to the very lowest possible cost. This country has followed the practice of assisting the manufacturer to enable him to compete in the markets of the world by giving him drawbacks on his raw material. It is only following out the same policy to the farming community in this country to reduce the cost of their implements of production.
As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has said, all the facts on this matter are not yet known, yet enough is known, it seems to me. for us, at all events for myself, to come to the conclusion-and I doubt very much if the facts that are left to be brought out will change it-that the interests of western Ca-
nada and the interests of the farmers all over Canada, and particularly of western Canada, where grain is handled, as the hon. member for Macleod has said, largely with the motor truck demand a reduction of the duties, and this is one of the places where a reduction can be made that will be of benefit to the farming community.
I do not know whether the mover of the resolution and I would agree upon the point I am now going to mention. If I remember rightly, some of his colleagues in that corner of the house, not so many years ago, spoke rather disparagingly of the work done by the tariff board. I am inclined to think that the hon. member for Macleod, from the information that he has been able to gather as to the work done by the tariff board, would now feel like commending its work. It is bringing out very valuable information. Matters of this nature are being treated openly, and the information elicited is enabling the house and the country at large to see more clearly the effects of the tariff.
Speaking more particularly of the western farmer, I may say that he finds himself in such a position that the holding of land during the past year or two, because of his difficulties in the way of frost, rust and plant diseases, has brought him to the point where -perhaps it may be putting it a little extremely-it is a question whether the ownership of land is an asset or a liability. Now, if that were the case only with those who are poor farmers, who have allowed their land to become dirty and are inefficient in their work, I think there would be little ground for complaint. The quicker those farmers were replaced by better men the better it would be for them and for the country. But, as a matter of fact the time has arrived when even efficient, capable, able-bodied farmers, men who are handling their jobs as well as those engaged in any other line of work, find themselves in a position where it is next to impossible for them to make a living, even though they have good farms. Naturally their buying power is decreased. They are not able to take the goods of the manufacturers, they are not able to sustain those who are engaged in industrial work in the cities, and consequently the plants are closed down, leading to unemployment. If the farmer were *working on a basis where he could make a fair profit, he would be buying more goods and his money would filter through to those in other industries, which would help the railways, the storekeepers, and others.
I am entirely in sympathy with this resolution. I might add that the farmers, particularly of western Canada, and I believe in

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) remarked that he was surprised that the hon. gentlemen to our right had not risen in protest against a resolution of this kind. As a matter of fact I would have been very much surprised if they had, for I feed that they understand, at least subconsciously, that the interests of the manufacturers are perfectly safe in the capable hands of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). So far as I am personally concerned, I subscribe neither to the shibboleth of high protection nor to the shibboleth of free trade. I stand for equal protection to all or no protection to anybody. If the present or any other administration can give protection to the agriculturist equal to that which they give to the manufacturers, I am satisfied with tariffs; if they cannot do that, then the time has come for them to wipe out tariffs entirely.
That is the principle upon which I wish to make a few remarks on this resolution. I think the hon. gentleman who introduced it (Mr. Coote) has made it very clear indeed, in fact has demonstrated its soundness by figures. He took those figures from that body which the Minister of Finance tells us has been entrusted with the examination of this very problem,, and by those figures he has shown that as a result of the tariff protection which this industry enjoys, the manufacture of motor cars and motor trucks is a very profitable business. He shows also this strange anomaly, that motor -cars and motor trucks produced in this country are dearer to Canadians than they are to any other people in the world. He indicates also that the manufacturers in their own interests not only take advantage of the protection which they enjoy to raise their prices, but they also take advantage of freight rates. Further, he shows that at all points this industry is perfectly capable of taking care of itself without any protection at all, and even quotes such an authority as Mr. Henry Ford to that effect. Then the hon. gentleman asks that the trucks-just the tracks-be classified as regards tariff with farm wagons and similar farm implements.
Now, sir, we thought-at least I thought, and I am sure other hon. members have thought so too-that this resolution was a very timely one. Timely because, first of all, the budget has not yet been brought down, and if there is any meaning at all in parliamentary procedure I thought that the representations of hon. members would be taken into consideration in a serious way; and if that is to be done the time to consider our viewpoint is now before the budget is brought down, for experience has taught us- and indeed the Minister of Finance has just proved it-that if we wait until the budget is brought down, brought down in a way that is regarded as proper and constitutional, then everything is fixed and whatever we may saj' is not even considered, no alterations have ever been made. To make such alterations on the advice of any member not sitting on the government benches would be to admit weakness on the part of the administration, and to force changes by a vote would mean the defeat of the government. So that under the circumstances we are absolutely helpless to effect any change if we wait until the budget comes down. Therefore, if our presence here is to mean anything at all, hon. members must be permitted to express their opinions on fiscal matters before the budget has been brought down.
Also, we thought this resolution was timely, because a resolution dealing with reductions of tariffs on automobiles was brought forward, I think in 1926, by the same hon. gentleman and resulted in whatever reductions were made at that time. Then there is another reason why we thought it was a timely resolution: we believed that the new Minister of Finance was in favour of tariff reduction. Indeed, I think he is on record as having made such a declaration as recently as a few weeks ago when he was in the west. With that assurance we thought this an acceptable time to bring forward suggestions for a reduction of the duty in respect to motor trucks, feeling that we had a real friend at court who would sympathize with the appeal of the western farmers for such a picayune reduction as would be implied in this resolution. And surely when we considered the protection enjoyed by the manufacturers of motor cars and motor trucks in relation to the protection that the farmers get, we felt that we were not going too far when we asked that motor trucks be placed in the same tariff schedule as farm wagone. Feeling therefore that the minister was sincere in his declaration we thought this was a timely resolution.

I just returned to the house a few minutes ago from my home, and had not thought any such resolution woidd come before this house. Had it not been for the very pointed, though extremely kindly, remarks of my hon. friend from Saskatoon (Mr. Young) across the way I certainly would have left the responsibility of action in this matter with the government of the day to whom, I consider, such matters should be justly left. But I am compelled to say this: It matters not to me whether or not all the members of this house are unanimous upon this occasion; so far as I am concerned, I am opposed to the resolution because of two facts.
My hon. friend has referred a good many times in this house to a deputation of honest, hard-working people who came all the way from the city of Oshawa to the city of Ottawa to point out to this government that tampering with the tariff in regard to this great industry would prejudice their homes and their callings in life. Let me tell my hon. friend that I was home over the past week end, and those people who were in procession to the hill at Ottawa are in procession now looking for jobs. Hundreds of them are being supplied with relief in the city of Oshawa because they are out of work; others are working one or two hours each day, some four hours, some three days a week, and yet on the statistics compiled by the bureau in the city of Ottawa they are placed in the class of employed. They

are employed just sufficient to keep poverty from their doors. When these gentlemen were here, when that procession of honest Canadians seeking to protect their homes and their jobs came to Ottawa, what were they told? They were told by the Prime Minister of Canada to go home and devote themselves to the reading of the 19th chapter of the Acts of the Apostles, which described them as so many thousands of heathens in a rage coming to this city to importune the great apostle, asking him to save them, and shouting " O, great is Diana of the Ephesians." This was all the sympathy handed out to those people on that occasion. I ask my hon. friend from Saskatoon whether a man who is a Canadian in an industrial city is not worthy of the same consideration from this country as any other citizen. Are the people who are employed in the upbuilding of the industries of this country to have the ground cut from beneath their feet every year or two? If my hon. friend will look at the statistics since that memorable procession to Ottawa, he will find this: that the imports of automobiles into this country have increased to-day over 300 per cent. Had the tariff been left as Sir Wilfrid Laurier put it when he was Prime Minister of this country, in the city of Oshawa to-day there would be three months' extra work at ten hours per day, instead of conditions as we now find them. Yet we are asked to pay no attention to such a state of affairs, but to decrease, still decrease, the meagre allowance of industrial protection there is left to our people.
Mr. Speaker, this question may be before the house on another occasion, when I will en-reavour to have available further facts. All that -I ask parliament to do at the present time, and I , plead with parliament, is to leave this question where it ought to be. First, have every fact investigated before the tariff board which has been appointed and which is assumedly functioning, and then leave to the government of the day the terrible responsibility of wiping out a new industry in this country and of demolishing a promising young city of Canada. That is all I ask parliament to do. I do not think for one moment that every hon. member on this side of the house is in favour of smashing the industrial fabric of this Dominion of Canada.

Therefore I think the hon. member for Prince would be quite in order if he would agitate among his own party for the adoption of their own platform, and then we shall have motor trucks down to the point where there will be no duty whatever on them.
Last session we had the pleasing experience of having the Minister of Finance reduce the duty on combines from 10 per cent to 6 per cent. It would not be unfair to aim at having the duty on motor trucks on a par with that on combines. If the party in power does not see its way clear to go all the way with their own platform, they should at least recognize the fact that the motor truck is just as necessary as the combine, because the two go together. Last session we adopted the principle of reducing the duty on the combine from 10 per cent to 6 per cent, putting it on a par with the binder. It is an agricultural implement and we put it in the same class as the self-harvester-binder. Recognizing the fact that the motor truck is necessary to go with the combine, if we cannot get the motor truck free, let us aim at reducing the duty on it, not merely to 10 per cent, which is the duty at which wagons are at present listed, but down to 6 per cent, thus putting it on a par with the combine. I am quite sure, if the minister is convincible, he will easily see that this would be a benefit to the agricultural industry of western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, may I say a word in favour of this resolution? It states that the motor truck at the present time is taking the place of the wagon in the delivery of grain to market. That is very true, but that is not the only use to which the motor truck is being put. My hon. friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael), who has just taken his seat, stated that the motor truck should go in combination with the combine. That is also very true, but even where the combine is not in use, it is necessary that motor trucks should be available to the farmers at lower prices.

When we realize what it costs to-day to furnish storage on the farm, we can understand that it is very necessary that the farmers who produce grain, even though they have not a combine, should get their grain to market, get it away to the elevators, of which they are now building many, rather than be put to the expense of furnishing storage on their farms. In western Canada the governments are entering extensively into the business of constructing roads. In the matter of surfacing roads, hauling gravel and so on, the motor truck has put the wagon and the old grey mare out of business. If the farmers are to get a part of that work, that is, of constructing their own roads, it is necessary that they should possess motor trucks.
My hon. friend across the way, in making a plea for increased labour for the residents of his community, overlooked the question: unless you can increase the purchasing power of the patrons of that industry, how are you going to increase production? The only way you can increase production is by increasing the purchasing power of the users of those implements. It has been said in the speech from the throne that Canada is very prosperous. I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, from firsthand knowledge, that there is not very much prosperity to-day among the agriculturists of Canada, and unless the cost of production is lowered there will be many men out of agriculture before very long. This is only one way in which agricultural production can be stimulated. This resolution simply asks that the duty be lowered to equal that on other lines of agricultural machinery. I think it is a fair request and that the government should accede to it.

In regard to the two
resolutions to which the Minister of Finance has directed attention, it will be seen at once that they are not in the same category. The

Tariff on Motor Trucks-Mr. Bennett
resolution to be moved by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) deals with an entirely different matter from that under consideration. He suggests that consideration should be given by the government to defraying part of the cost of establishing health units. He could not express the matter in another way, because the initiative must be taken by the administration, so all he suggests is that the government should give consideration to the initiation of that policy.
As regards the resolution under discussion, it seems to me it is competent for the House of Commons, disregarding party differences, and dealing with the question merely as members of parliament, to express the opinion that the government of the day should take definite action. That is what this resolution proposes. Whether or not that action should be taken depends upon our conception of the situation in Canada and whether or not we have made up our minds that we desire to establish and maintain a motor industry in the Dominion.
The first question that, it seems to me, must be answered, is: Shall we have a motor industry in Canada? Arising out of that question you have the collateral or complementary question as to whether or not that motor industry shall limit its operations to otheT forms of motor vehicles than trucks or whether it shall extend its operations to the manufacture of trucks. If we conclude that we shall have a motor industry in this country, the only method whereby it can be established is by its being given an equal opportunity with its competitors in other lands. That is why recourse has been had to the tariff in days gone by. We have afforded the motor industry an opportunity to become established in Canada. That opportunity has been, it is true, afforded by a. tariff. In 1926 it was suggested that the tariff was too high, but the protection afforded to the motor industry by the action taken by the government at that time is not less than that which it enjoyed before the tariff was amended. Any hon. gentleman who will take the figures and make the computations n-eed have no doubt with respect to that.
As to whether or not we should have as a branch of that motor industry a motor truck industry, is a matter about which there may be a difference of opinion. For my own part, and I believe I speak for the great majority of Canadians, I think that we should so far as within us lies endeavour to produce within uhis country not only the implements of production, but everything that may be necessary to render us not dependent upon other people for the ability to till our fields, cut and manufacture our forest products, and carry
on the development of our resources. Holding that view, as I believe the majority of Canadians do, it follows that the question I have just asked-shall we maintain our motor truck industry in Canada?-should be answered in the affirmative.
How shall that industry be maintained? It cannot be said that it can compete on equal terms with its competitors in the United States if it is to depend entirely in its early struggles upon itself under the conditions as they exist and without some form of action being taken by parliament that will place that industry on an equality with the industry which enjoys the great market to the south. There you have the greatest motor truck producing industry in the world. There you have the greatest domestic market. There you have a country with the largest export market for motor trucks in the world. We Canadians have concluded-it is too late now for us to say that we will go back upon our determination-that we will establish a motor and motor truck industry in Canada. Having so decided, the question is whether or not we shall now wreck that industry or continue it as a branch of our productive industrial life.
I confess, Mr. Speaker, that I did endeavour, as my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) has done, to ascertain three facts: (I) How many motor trucks did we make in Canada last year; (2) to what extent were these motor trucks manufactured in Canada as distinguished from being a mere assembling of parts imported from other countries; (3) to what extent were we able to supply (a) our domestic requirements, and Ob) the export market. Owing to the very difficulties to which my hon. friend from Macleod has referred I have been unable to satisfy myself upon these points, and I am bound to say that the observations made by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) have left the matter still in doubt, as indeed did the explanation given by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm).
Under these circumstances I submit with all frankness that this house is not in a position to arrive at a definite conclusion on the motion which is now submitted for its consideration. It would be unfair to jeopardize, through lack of knowledge to enable us to exercise a sound judgment, the existence of an industry in this country which we have concluded shall be a branch of our industrial life. On the other hand, I am perfectly satisfied that if this house had the necessary information to enable it to arrive at an accurate conclusion, it would have no hesitancy in pronouncing its judgment, whatever it may be; and realizing as I now do from the observations made
Tariff on Motor Trucks-Division

by every member of this house who has spoken on the resolution that no member is able to speak upon it with any degree of authority because he has before him no recommendation from the tariff board and no precis of facts as to what the result upon the motor truck industry would be should this resolution become effective, I have concluded that the tariff board should be afforded the opportunity to complete its investigations and make known to this house through the proper channels the conclusions at which it has arrived. If there has been exploitation of the consumer, on the one hand, I am sure that that can be remedied by this parliament. On the other hand, if it is true that the protection now afforded is no more than sufficient to enable the industry to be continued in this country, surely there is no man in this house who is disposed to destroy it. Under these circumstances, awaiting the further reports that may be made by the tariff board I propose to move the adjournment of the debate, and to defer my further observations until that information is available. I therefore move the adjournment of the debate.

subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS

speakeroldname: Mr. H. E. SPENCER (Battle River) moved:
subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of making grants to the provinces equal to one-third the cost of establishing, and to cover permanently such full time health units as may be organized.
He said: Mr. Speaker, tlhe subject of this resolution is, I think, one of the most important that we have to consider in Canada today. I am asking that the government take into consideration the advisability of making grants to the provinces to help in carrying on full time health units, that is, a form of organization to care for the public health.
These full time health units are not by any means a new development om the North American continent, for I find that in the United States they have no less than 337 established, and of later years they have invaded Canada in the provinces of Quebec and British Columbia. I understand also that the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba are anticipating organizing to take advantage of this development.
I should like to bring before the house a resolution passed quite recently at the annual convention of the United Farm Women of Alberta. It is in these words:
Whereas, it is expedient that preventable disease and death in the rural areas of Canada be more efficiently controlled, and
Whereas, full time rural health units have been 'found effective for such purposes in certain provinces of -Canada, and States of the United States of America, and
Whereas, under the [present organization of such units the Rockefeller Foundation will bear for a period of only three years ome-third of the cost of such units;
Be it therefore resolved, that the federal government, through the Minister of National Health at Ottawa, be requested to provide a grant to the provinces of Canada, sufficient to cover permanently the one-third share of the cost of sueh rural health units.
A similar resolution, I understand, has been passed by other public bodies, particularly by organizations that have undertaken the care of public health in rural districts. It is in these districts that such care is most necessary, because for the most part the municipal authorities in our cities have been able to look after
the city population much better than it has been possible to take care of those living in our rural districts. We are realizing to-day that the conservation of the health of the people is of the greatest importance, for although the people are the greatest national asset, those who fail to retain their health very soon become liabilities. Undoubtedly there is no greater worry, particularly to parents, than the fear of sickness and their inability to give their families proper medical care, or to pay the cost of medical care or hospital treatment. We are told that education is of first importance. It certainly is, because ignorance is very detrimental to any community, province or Dominion; but without health what is the good of education? Health, therefore, should be the basis of education. It is the basis of sucess; it is the basis of happiness, and it is the basis of the very best you can get out of life.
The minimum staff necessary for one of these health units will be a medical officer, a public health nurse, a sanitary inspector and a secretary. The area covered by each health unit, comprises usually about six municipal units, serving a territory of 2,000 square miles, which would comprise a population of some 2,200 to 2,500 people. That, of course, would vary according to the particular province in which these health units might be organized and the density of population in area concerned. It would be necessary to set up a public laboratory in each of these districts, the facilities of which-this is most important-would be utilized for the prevention and control of disease. Quantities of vaccine and serum could be kept in the laboratories, which could be given out if necessary to the various practising -physicians. I believe that one of these units could be operated for a sum varying from $12,000 to $20,000. That may seem quite a large amount, but it is not very large considering the fact that the unit covers such a large area. The suggestion is that the cost be divided between the municipalities making up the unit and the provincial government, each paying one third. One-third at present is being paid -by the Rockefeller foundation. Unfortunately the Rockefeller foundation pays its one-third for only three years, but we should consider ourselves very fortunate indeed that such an organization should encourage and indeed make possible the formation of such health units. From either the provincial or the federal point of view, health is recognized as -being of tremendous importance; we ha-ve evidence of that in the existence of a Dominion Department of Health. All we are asking in this resolution is that as these organizations are formed, and as in
National Health-Mr. Spencer

the course of time the Rockefeller foundation withdraw from further payments for the carrying on of this splendid work elsewhere, the federal government should come to their assistance 'by paying one third of the cost of their establishment. We sometimes hear criticism of the americanization of Canada, but there ;s one instance where we are very glad indeed to accept the help that is offered to us, particularly in the matter of care of public health. We cannot expect that to continue forever, and it can be said that if they wish to withdraw at the end of three years they have at least done a tremendous amount of good, not only contributing a third of the cost for each of the three years, but making it possible to start other units in Canada.
To give some idea of the value of these health organizations I would like to refer to what has been done in this connection in the province of Quebec. A health unit was established there about three years ago. During 1926 there were 643 deaths from general causes in the district served by it. Last year the figure dropped to 487, a saving of 156 lives. Infantile mortality dropped from 213 to 160; deaths from tuberculosis from 56 to 51, and deaths from contagious diseases from 86 to 27. Doctor Alphonse Lessard, director of the Quebec bureau of health and Dr. Emile Nadeau, assistant director of the same department, make the following statement:
In countries where health units have been in operation for a period of two or three years, the general death rate has been reduced and especially the infantile mortality, and the death rate for contagious and infectious diseases; with also a marked reduction in the number of eases, this being largely due to better education of the public and immediate control of epidemics,
Dr. H. E. Young, provincial health officer for British Columbia, states that in a single year, through the functioning of a county health unit, one community saved $6,000 in isolation hospital fees.
In citing these facts I am sure I will be supported by hon. members who have had the 'experience of starting up in a pioneer country, as many of us have done in western Canada, and have had to face the problem of the maintenance of health, not only the problem of taking care of the sick, but that of getting the wherewithal to pay the physicians. It is an easy matter to pay a small annual amount by way of tax, as a sort of insurance, to take care of health, but it is a very difficult and a very serious matter for probably seventy or eighty .per cent of the people to have to pay a large doctor or hospital bill when they are sick. Not only is the present system bad I Mr. Spencer.]
for the individual but it is also bad for the medical profession, and I (believe from what I have been told by men in the medical profession, particularly in the rural districts, that more and more such organizations are coming into favour. I understand that the present Minister of Health is very sympathetic to the idea of these health units, and from the discussion had in this house only a year ago I feel sure that a large number of hon. members are very anxious indeed that something should be done by the federal government in the matter of taking greater care of the health of the people of Canada. I am therefore going to ask that this resolution be thoroughly discussed, and I hope it will receive the hearty support of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when
the house adjourned at six o'clock my hon friend from Battle River (Mr. Spencer) had concluded his address on a very importan; subject, one which has attracted a good deai of attention on the part of public bodies throughout Canada. As a minister of the crown I have received petitions from various organizations and from two provincial governments suggesting that it would be advisable and in the interests of the health of the public that the Dominion government should make a contribution towards the establishment of health units throughout Canada. As my hon. friend said, the idea of properly organized health units is not new; in the larger municipalities and cities of Canada and throughout the world they have for years had properly organized departments which looked after the public health of the municipality or district. Unfortunately in this important matter, the people in the rural constituencies have not been able to advance as rapidly as the larger centres, probably due to the lack of knowl-

National Health-Mr. King (Kootenay)
edge and interest on the part of the public in the rural centres and the fact that they live a freer life and are not exposed to the dangers of congestion which exist in the larger districts.
But an unusual situation has occurred. It has been found by people who have studied this question that men or women can live in the larger centres with betteT opportunities for health than exist in rural centres. That was not thought to be the fact some years ago; in fact, I am satisfied that if you go into the congested areas to-day you will find the people saying, "We wish we could go to the country where we could get fresh air and the greater opportunities for health that there prevail." It is necessary to study the real cause of that situation. There is no doubt those who are living in the rural districts have better opportunities to enjoy good health and longevity than those who live in the congested areas, but it has come to be known scientifically, through the employment in the department of full-time men to consider the advantages of certain health measures, that in the cities the people do in some respects enjoy better conditions than those of the rural districts.
The resolution before us suggests that the federal government should contribute certain financial support to the provincial governments and they, in turn, to the municipalities or units that may be established. My hon. friend from Battle River to-day reviewed the history of the rural units throughout the United States and Canada. The federal government of the United States became involved in this question during the time of the Mississippi flood, which occurred some two or three years ago. Here they were faced with a national catastrophe that was beyond the control of the local authorities, and it became necessary for the federal bureau of health to adopt certain health measures. The federal authorities of the United States did so, and were able to show through their central organization that it was possible to prevent the great epidemics which might have arisen in that country after the flood. Their experience showed that proper organization and proper attention to the matter on the part of men qualified to deal with such questions can do a great deal to prevent contagion and disease.
Then we have the advantage of the experience gained from the great war, when large groups of men were confined in barracks and camps under what might be considered almost impossible conditions. But owing to improved sanitation and the care taken by health
authorities these men enjoyed splendid health and were in excellent condition. In the year of the influenza epidemic the men who were in camp, under proper medical conditions, did not suffer as greatly as the civilian population. With that experience and a more educated public-because the public has become more educated through the advancement of our educational institutions-we have to-day a real demand by the people of this country for better health measures in the rural municipalities. This is a natural demand and one that should receive the attention of public men, but we as the Dominion parliament in viewing this question must consider our place in the government of this great country. We are carrying on the government of Canada under what is known as the British North America Act, which states definitely that matters pertaining to education and health shall be dealt with locally. At page 436 of Beauchesne you will find the subjects reserved to the Dominion and under their control, and section 11 includes:
Quarantine and the establishment and maintenance of marine hospitals.
Then we find the exclusive powers of provincial * legislatures stated also. Section 7 says:
The establishment, maintenance amd management of hospitals, asylums, charities, eleemosynary institutions in and for the province, other than marine hospitals.
There seems to have been a desire on the part of those who framed our constitution to give to the people of the provinces local control, which I think is very essential in health matters. Now, it may be suggested that we should continue to leave the control locally with the municipalities or provinces. I am sure that if the Dominion government should enter this field they wovdd be a party to granting money in the expenditure of which they had no control and no say. Many public bodies have come to Ottawa asking that we invade the provincial field and give subsidies and make grants, but the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has made himself very well understood by stating that the principle is vicious. If we sat down and considered this matter seriously, I think we would agree with that statement. Regarding the interference with provincial health matters in voting subsidies or granting money, we have not only the statement of the Prime Minister but also the statement made in 1928 by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) during the course of a debate upon a matter affecting international health, namely the International Sanitary Convention. A smallpox epidemic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I at the outset congratulate the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) for having introduced this important subject for the consideration of parliament, and allow me also to congratulate the hon. minister (Mr. King, Kootenay), for having gone as far as

National Health-Mr. Garland (Bow River)
he has in admitting the need, although I am sorry that he ended as he did, disclaiming responsibility. The need for such relief as is covered by this resolution has been laid before the house by two hon. members and there is not much I can add, but I will try to interest the house for a few moments.
In my province the provincial Department of Health undertook some real progressive action a few years ago when they established what we know as the travelling school clinics. The school districts organized in groups of three or four and one schoolhouse is turned into a sort of temporary hospital. The mothers bring bedding, beds are set up, and what amounts to a travelling health unit arrives. This consists of a qualified doctor or two, some nurses, and the assistance of local help. I am reminded that a dentist always accompanies the party. These school clinics have in my opinion, done more for Canada in recent years than any other single factor. They have taken young people who otherwise would have been crushed and thwarted in youth-twisted, deformed, warped, stunted, misunderstood,-and made worthwhile Canadian citizens of them. The Minister of National Health knows the effect upon a human body of what may appear to be a minor ailment in youth, something wrong with the tonsils, adenoids, eyes, ears. The child is in school, declared to be stupid, vicious, stubborn, when as a matter of fact none of these things is true; all that is wrong with the child is that some physical defect is present. If this is taken in proper time and cured, the mental and physical development immediately begins to become progressive and the child develops into a healthy and more valuable citizen. In the operation of these school clinics, through the generosity of the physicians, whenever time permitted the examination of adults also took place, and arising out of that examination we discovered, especially in the newer areas in my province, an astonishing number of adults who urgently needed medical attention to a minor or major degree. It brought home to us more clearly than anything else could have done the absolute necessity for some kind of health unit, travelling or stationary, in Canada. Personally I think that if we apply the establishment of these to our .country, we shall find that the travelling variety will be more acceptable to the rural areas, but that is a detail than can be dealt with later.
The question is then asked among our people: Since we find the examination and cure of minor defects well worth while, a blessing greater than others that have come to us in
recent years, why not apply the same thing in a more complete fashion to adults also? If I had my way; if I could influence the administration of the various governments in this country, it would be not merely to establish health units, but to make available to every human being in Canada free medical examination once every year. Hon. members sitting opposite and around me think it is good business to take a piece of iron and tin and paint to an expert once a year for an overhaul; yet when we consider the marvellous delicacy of the human body, the slightest derangement of the organization of which may enormously affect the physical health and usefulness to the state of the individual, there can be no question in our minds that if it be good to examine a machine of tin and iron once a year in order that it shall be effective, it is a thousand times more necessary that the human body should have available as thorough a.n examination.
In our rural areas you may find, and indeed medical men will give you the evidence quite freely, that there are thousands of adults who deliberately refrain either because of distance from doctors, or because of cost, from having that annual examination which is so necessary. There are others who refrain even when they know they are sick and leave medical care to the last possible moment, until in desperation, in fear of very death itself, they at last appeal, frequently too late to the doctor. It is that condition of affairs that we desire to remedy, and 'that is why, just as the minister has admitted, we find in recent years a steady growth of public opinion, demanding recognition by the state of the state's responsibilities in this regard to its citizens.
Let us see whether we .can show more clearly than by mere statements of opinions the urgent need for this remedy. Out of the war there arose one valuable result at least, that is a more complete set of statistics, dealing with the medical health of the soldiers, than we had ever had before. During the period prior to the bringing into effect of the Military Service Act there were 465,984 voluntary enlistments. Of these 74,963 or nearly 75,000 weTe stricken off the roils as medically unfit. This is contained in a letter from General MadBrien to Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, M.P., under date of January 13, 1925. Of the balance, the 300,000 odd, General Sir Arthur Currie, speaking in Montreal on September 12, 1924, before the Taxation and Civil Service convention, said:
Something like 100,000 men went overseas who were physically unfit for service and cost the country some $150,000,000.
The report of that speech is contained in the Ottawa Citizen of September 13, 1924.

Let us come to the period after the Military Service Act amd we find that the total number of applicants for enlistment was 264,355. Of that number only 83,355 were accepted and 181.000, or 68 per cent, were rejected. I do not wish to exaggerate, and I am ready to admit at once that many of the physical defects from which these rejected suffered were not such as to have incapacitated them from civilian activities, but on the other hand a groat portion of them did suffer from defects that handicapped their usefulness to themselves and to the nation. Let me emphasize again another point: these men were not the aged and the infirm or the very young. They were men in the prime of life, in the finest years of manhood. And yet we find that appalling percentage declared to be unfit for military service. No further evidence ought to be required by hon. members than that to signify the extraordinary necessity for state recognition of its responsibilities for the health of its citizens.
But I will give just one more illustration. Turning to the Canada Year Book for 1927-28, at page 942 and otheT pages, I find the following striking information. The number of fully constituted universities in Canada is twenty-three; the number of insane asylums in Canada is fifty-two. There are more than twice as many insane asylums in Canada as there are universities. We now take the question of first-year admissions to both these types of institutions, and we find in the year 1925-26 there entered Canadian universities a total of 3,326, while there were placed in insane institutions 6,301. We take the total number of inmates of universities and the total number of inmates of insane asylums, and we find that occupants of universities totalled that year 9,525 and of insane asylums nearly three times as many, or 25,259. This is bad enough, but it does not tell the whole story. There is not an hon. member that does not know that there is not a province in Canada at this moment, except possibly Prince Edward Island, that is not in crying need of mere facilities for the greater care of the mentally defective. I am also satisfied that if we could have this annual examination, if we could make available to our people cheap but efficient medical attention, it would enormously reduce the number of those who through some minor defect gradually develop a neurotic condition which leads them on to nervous disorders often resulting in breakdown and causing them to become at least temporary inmates of mental asylums.
Now I come to the hon. minister's closing remarks. I expected that he would ring in 
the good old British North America Act and the responsibility of the [provinces. Mr. Speaker, in a question of this kind, involving the most vital part -of life itself, that is health, I say that those who drafted the constitution either have been misunderstood or should now be reinterpreted if they meant to say that the federal government bad no responsibility in the matter. I will go further. I just happened to turn up the estimates shortly after dinner this evening, and I find on page 21 that the federal government is providing to expend on health of animals, $2,550,000. Why, if we had that much to devote to the purpose of this resolution we would be satisfied with that as a commencement for this year. I turn now to page 62 of the estimates, providing for expenditure under Pensions and National Health, in order *to find what is the contribution under the constitution of the federal government to national health. Separate the items that are devoted solely to pensions and care of soldiers -by the way it is interesting to note that the constitution is wide enough to enable the federal government to contribute to the health welfare of a soldier who has again become a civilian, and who is no longer an employee of the federal government, but it is not wide enough to embrace the rest of humanity in the country. That puzzles me. However, I will take only the items that almost hit you in the eye as you look at them. For the administration of the acts respecting food and drugs, including the Laboratory of hygiene, there is provided $163,500; for pollution of inland waters and Public Works Health Act, $26,000; for marine hospitals, including burial expenses of destitute deceased mariners and grants to institutions assisting sailors, $250,000.
I have no doubt that that includes -more than health; it includes assistance to sailors, so I am being rather liberal in the 'estimate that I shall make in a moment. I cannot for the life O'f me understand why the fathers of confederation decided' that it was advisable the state should be responsible for the health of these sailors and not for the health of the rest, of the citizens of the country. Compare that with $2,500,000 for the health of animals.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to refer to one point raised by the Minister of Health (Mr. King, Kootenay). While I was a member of the provincial board of health in the province of Ontario we took the ground that the Dominion parliament had the prime responsibility in regard to public health. We submitted the question to a distinguished jurist, Mr. Justice Riddell, now of the Supreme 'Court of Ontario. His opinion was that the responsibility for the public health of the Dominion rested with the Dominion government. These were his reasons for reaching that opinion. Public health as understood to-day 'had no existence in 1867. The first effort to provide public health in the Dominion was in 1882, when the Liberal government in the province of Ontario placed at the head of its health department the distinguished Doctor Bryce. The science of preventive medicine not being known in 1867, the British North America Act could not possibly deal with it. That act provided that hospitals, asylums, and eleemosynary or charitable institutions should be assigned to the provinces, but the only thing that was known in regard to public health at that time was the matter of quarantine. Quarantine was assigned to the exclusive jurisdiction of the Dominion parliament.

Public health matters, as I say, are not exclusively assigned to the provinces by the British North America Act and as public health men we believe that the Dominion must necessarily play its part in this work. It should be remembered that hospitals and asylums are intended to take care of those people who are sick and to cure them. The great object of public health work is to prevent people from becoming sick, but preventive medicine as understood to-day as a science was unknown in 1867, the only thing in connection with public health at that time being, I repeat, quarantine, and this was assigned to the Dominion parliament. We believe that if to-day the fathers of confederation were drawing up a new charter for Canada, public health would be regarded as a national undertaking the same as it is in England, France, the United States and in every other civilized country in the world.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not like to let this occasion pass without saying a word in support of the motion of the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer). Full time health units do not differ essentially from the ordinary municipal health units; they are composed of a board of health, a health officer, a health inspector and a secretary, differing from the ordinary municipal unit in that the health unit is composed of several municipalities, which pay fifty per cent of the cost. Twenty-five per cent of the cost is borne by the provincial government, and the remaining 25 per cent by the Rockefeller foundation.
The government takes the attitude that this should be a purely provincial matter, and that for one reason or another the federal government is not in a position to make a grant towards this enterprise. I maintain .that the health of Canada is of first importance and should be the first consideration of the Canadian government. Whatever view pray lhave been taken of this subject by the fathers of confederation, I do not think it can be questioned for one moment that the health of the Canadian people is one of the most important considerations of the Canadian government. For that reason I do not see how the government can avoid-if I may use that expression-participating in this matter.
The purpose of full time health units is to reach the newer, sparsely settled rural areas where there are few doctors and no nurses. There is no doubt that the people in these areas have a crying need for medical service. In Manitoba, the oldest of the western provinces, there is dire need of medical service, and there are many districts where there are no medical men. Manitoba, with its narrow river farms, its clustered villages, its small quarter-section farms, contains many districts in need of medical service. Every province has a flourishing medical college turning out in large numbers young medical men of a very good type; other medical men cross the ocean from the old country, but still our country districts are in need of medical attention. I suppose the reason is that most medical men prefer to remain in tlhe cities, and then there is the factor to be considered that in the outermost rural districts it is very
22S

National Health-Mr. Adshead
difficult for the average doctor to make a living. If he is not substantially assisted by the municipality it is very difficult for him to live. There is another factor which is worthy of consideration, and that is the taking up by American rural districts of the graduates from our medical schools. It is not difficult for a Canadian medical graduate to obtain a livelihood in a thriving and progressive settlement in the States, and for that reason the rural districts of Canada have to suffer.
At the beginning of this century the death rate in Canada per thousand was 19 in the cities and 15.2 in the country. The difference is not surprising because the people in the city were exposed to infection, contagion, and accidents which were not so prevalent in the country. Twenty years after the opening of the century the urban rate had fallen to 13 per thousand while the rural rate had fallen to 14. The reason is very obvious. Health boards, health inspectors, health regulations, and proper supervision in the cities have been responsible for this improvement.
This matter has been a burning question throughout Canada, and a few days ago I received a memorial from the Confederated Women's Institute of Canada. They adopted a series of hypotheses, and I could not do better than to read them to -the house. They were as follows:
Whereas it has been proven that the cost of unnecessary illness and death in Canada is very great, amounting to millions of dollars and thousands of lives annually.
And whereas, it has been amply demonstrated, particularly in the larger cities, that full-time health service results in an immediate fall in sickness and death rates.
And whereas, in most rural communities the people have been forced to rely upon the parttime services of physicians for the carrying on of community health measures-an arrangement which is at best ineffective.
And whereas, the most satisfactory method of securing results in rural and small urban areas as regards the control of communicable disease and the reduction of general mortality rates has been demonstrated in Quebec, British Columbia and many states in the United States to be by means of the county health unit-
This would correspond to our Canadian full-time health units.
-such units supporting a full-time health office, sanitary inspector, public health nurse and secretary.	_
And whereas, organized health conservation should he made applicable to the whole Dominion, it is probable that the achievement of such an ideal can only be made, possible by the financial participation of the Dominion government as in the case of successful venereal disease control scheme already in operation.

I repeat that I am entirely in accord with the motion of the hon. -member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) and I wish to congratulate him for having brought this matter before the house.
