speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with a great deal of attention to this debate, and I do not propose to add much to it for it would be trying to paint the lily or gild refined gold. A few days ago I stated that I believed in Liberal policies but I did not believe in Liberal practices. In order to refresh my memory I looked up some of the statements which were made at that notable convention of Liberals held in 1919. That was a very enthusiastic convention and when this question of national health arose the British North America Act did not seem to have any place in the discussion. There were present at that convention the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and they fell in line with the idea of a nation's health being federal business. The Liberal party ought not to forsake those policies now; they should not now shield themselves behind the British North America Act as the Minister of Health, Mr. King (Kootenay) has done, I would like to read some of the remarks made in those days, outlining some of the principles which they were not going to forsake. Speaking to the resolution as to national health, which I will read in a moment, the proposer said in part:
Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen: from the lips of orators, statesmen, politicians, public speakers all our lives, we have heard this statement, when the speaker has got worked up to a proper frenzy Oif oratory, "The citizen-the boy or the girl-is the nation's greatest asset." In our recollection they have immediately forgotten about it as soon as the echo has died away from the ring of sincerity. Immediately they have turned their attention to the standardizing of the physical well-being of pigs, and calves, and horses and other animals; to the conserving of forests; to raising the standard of agriculture-which is well and fitting and in its place, as it ministers to the welfare of the citizenship. But from a federal standpoint,-
That is the point I should like the house to note.
-they have entirely overlooked the conservation of the life of that citizenship.
Then the mover goes on to say:
As women, however, we have come to the convention with a clearly defined idea, and that is that the citizen is the basis of the nation's wealth; that the citizen is more important even than the production of wealth; and that what affects the welfare of the citizen and the life of the citizen is of primary importance.

National Health-Mr. MacLaren
Just before the resolution was put, this was said:
The great issue, in the opinion of the women at least, is that the Liberal party shall place in its .platform a plank, pledging itself to support vigorous, aggressive, public health measures with a view to conserving life and raising the standard of the physical efficiency of the citizens.
In order that there may be no doubt as to whether they thought this should be done by the provinces or not, the resolution speaks for itself, and I hope it will overcome the conscientious and scrupulous objection of the Minister of Health:
I have much .pleasure in moving the following resolution-
I believe, Mr. Speaker, you were present at this particular convention, as I see that fact mentioned.
-whereas human life and physical efficiency are the nation's greatest assets,-
Not the provinces.
-and whereas the conservation and improvement thereof should be the country's first care;
Therefore, this gathering of Liberals in convention assembled pledges itself to a vigorous prosecution of the measures best calculated to conserve the life and improve the physical standard of our Canadian citizenship.
I read this and make this short address just in order that the consciences and memories of my hon. friends on the other side may be somewhat revived and stimulated; and the objection which the minister has had in mind as regards the application of the British North America Act will surely disappear if he will consult his colleague the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), because the latter, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Speaker all supported the motion that the national health of the citizens was the nation's greatest asset, and certainly a matter of federal importance. I need scarcely mention the fact that the resolution carried.

speechtext:
The importance of the question of national health, of permanent health units and many other means of dealing with the prevention of disease and the promotion of public health, is very generally recognized. It needs no argument to press forward this most vital question, one of the most important that can be discussed. On the other hand, it has been regarded in the house that public health matters belong very largely to the provinces. It may be desirable to make a change at some time, but at present this is largely a provincial matter and we should view it as it stands to-day. I do not question for a moment the value of the discussion in the house, but at the same time I think we could get ahead
more rapidly if we proceeded in accordance with conditions as they are. Therefore I believe the proper procedure, the way to make the greatest advance, is to proceed through the provinces, and I ask these hon. members who have so admirably discussed the matter to-night whether there have been debates of this character in the provincial parliaments. Surely the members of the provincial parliaments will admit that this is a very important subject. If so, I would suggest that they obtain the initial action from the provinces and let them then come to the federal parliament. I believe that to a considerable extent we are directing our energies in the wrong direction. We are beginning with the federal parliament; we should begin with the provincial legislatures; let them approach the federal government and proceed in the direction of existing conditions with the prospect of obtaining some results. I do not think we can expect the federal government to take the first action, to be followed by the provinces. If the reverse process were followed, we would make better progress.

subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
I join with the hon, gentlemen who have preceded me in offering to the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) my sincere congratulations on having brought before the house this very important question. As has been said many times to-night, there is no matter of greater importance to a country as a whole than the health of its citizens. When I look over the resolution I find it hard to realize how we might value such work in terms of dollars and cents. It was said by one hon. member that if we spent as much from this parliament in connection with the health of human beings in Canada as we do for the health of sheep, cattle and swine, the provinces would be entirely satisfied. I quite agree with him in that regard, because it' would mean the addition of perhaps twenty-five per cent to what the provinces are already spending in this direction.
It is difficult to estimate the value of these health units and travelling clinics. In Ontario much work is being done along that line and in the few minutes during which I shall take up the time of the house I should like to mention a few of the potent facts coming to my attention. Some ten or twelve years ago the Department of Public Health at Toronto sent throughout the province a travelling exhibit showing the methods of contracting tuberculosis, also the methods of preserving milk and preparing food in a manner which would leave those articles free from tuberculosis. They had a moving picture

National Health-Mr. Maloney
machine which depicted these microscopic germs plainly on the canvas. They showed how a fly would come into contact with these germs and how the same fly would come into contact with many articles of food which we are daily using. They finally showed how that could foe prevented. Prior to that summer troubles with children, summer cholera, indigestion and gastric troubles of many kinds were common. To-day as a result of that exhibition summer gastric and intestinal troubles in children are really the exception. The mothers are deeply interested in familiarizing themselves with scientific methods of preparing infants' food, and the result is that throughout the greater part of this province to-day infant feeding is done in the proper manner. Then there is the proper treatment of milk and cream and the cleanliness connected with the manufacture of dairy butter. These things have placed Ontario butter ahead even of the New Zealand butter that is coming into this country by the millions of .pounds. These are a few of the results of that travelling exhibition.
In addition, we have to-day travelling clinics, dealing not only with the care and preparation of food, but with the examination of children at school and the examination of adults in the outlying parts of the province.
The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) gave a very clear outline of the many afflictions of childhood which might readily be cured or prevented, but which if neglected often resulted in the child becoming an incompetent citizen. In that he was quite right. The travelling clinics in Ontario have their school nurses, who go into the school and examine every child. They detect all the physical defects in that child, whether in relation to tonsils, adenoids, teeth or eyesight, and all these things are reported on. The clinic, if it is so desired, will remove the tonsils, attend to the teeth, and so forth, but never until the parents of the child are completely satisfied to have it done. The first and primary duty is to advise the parents. Prior to these clinics many of the parents who were able to pay for this medical service were unaware of the conditions that existed among the children, but as a result of the work of the clinics many children are today healthy who might otherwise have fallen into an enfeebled condition. Not only that, but goitre is also being treated by the public health authorities of this province, and the day will come when goitre will be unknown in Ontario. Similarly with the diseases of the chest, a most important mat-t-Mr. Maloney.]
ter in this and every other province1. The travelling clinics examine those suspected of having tuberculosis, those who have been exposed to the disease, and those known to be afflicted. An X-ray examination is given, anid the services of a specialist who travels around from place to place is made available to these people, whether they be rich or poor. There is no charge made. The result is that people are taught how t,o avoid tuberculosis, and those who have the disease in the incipient stage are warned and taught how to take care of themselves, so that in ninety-five per .cent of the .cases the disease never progresses. Those who are more seriously afflicted with the trouble are taught how to take care of themselves and are advised along proper lines. Much is being done in this way to stamp out that particular disease'.
Another affliction which unfortunately visited this province last year was infantile paralysis. Up to a few years ago, once an individual was afflicted with infantile paralysis he was either incapacitated for life or died. A bright, little child three or four or five years of age, active and happy, might one day be suddenly stricken down by infantile paralysis; the next day the child might be dead, or if he recovered would be left with one or two limbs, or perhaps all four, paralysed-a helpless invalid for life. But due to the efforts of the health authorities of the provinces the recent epidemic has left few or no marks. I believe great credit must be given to the province of Manitoba for the way in which they handled a veTy serious epidemic in that province two years ago. Following their experience, the outbreak of the disease in Ontario last year was well taken care of by the provincial health authorities, and the serum, which is the only known remedy, was distributed free throughout the province even to those who were in a position to pay for it. As a result of the activities of the provincial health department, the epidemic last year left few cripples in Ontario.
We have, in addition, the free distribution of insulin to those who are unable to pay for it. Insulin is doing great work and has saved many lives in the last few years.
I come to another important question, and that is maternal mortality. It is a fact that within the last year, and year after year, we have been losing from 7,000 to 9,000 or 10,000 mothers in Canada, mostly because of the fact that they have unskilled attendants, and because the mothers are untrained themselves in the care and treatment of their own case up to the time of birth. If the department of health of the provinces were in a position

National Health-Mr. McQuarrie
to send through the outlying districts someone to instruct 'very fully these prospective mothers, and mothers, in the methods of treatment and care necessary to prevent infection, maternal mortality would drop to a minimum. There is no reason why 9,000 mothers should lose their lives in this country each year as a result of maternity, and the sooner the government realizes that, the better, I am sure, it will be for them and for the country. The government must remember that the citizen of Canada is the property of the state, and it is the duty of this government to protect the citizen in every possible way.
State medicine has been mentioned to-night as the thing for Canada. That is not what is required at all. State medicine is not included in this resolution. This is merely asking for an advisory body, more by way of education for the people, and in the outlying districts, if necessary, for someone to act in behalf of the health of the people, and to act free of charge to those who are unable to procure a doctor.
In conclusion, may I say that the doctors in Canada are the most self-sacrificing body of men in the country. They are not only working themselves out of a job by endeavouring to procure information that will enable them to prevent disease of every character, but they have in the past fifteen years done more to abolish disease than any other class of people in the whole wide world have done to abolish their own particular work. In this way they sacrifice in many cases their means of existence, but they are prepared to go on sacrificing, and for that reason they are anxious that the federal government should add to the funds now being made available for the health of the people by provincial departments of health. I could tell you, Mr. Speaker, of the sacrifices that many doctors are making; I could tell you of doctors who travel by night and by day, over good and indifferent roads, in fair weather and foul, journeying twenty, thirty and forty miles to visit a patient, all without hope of gain or reward, simply because they are fulfilling a duty imposed upon them when they receive the degree of doctor of medicine, and that duty is to save life and ameliorate suffering wherever they can. That is what actuates every physician in the discharge of his duty. I say to this government, that if they will hand over to the provinces twenty-five per cent of what they are spending to-day on public health matters, I am sure that at the end of ten years, in the better health and increased happiness of the people, the expenditure will be repaid a thousandfold.

speechtext:
On many other occasions, Mr. Speaker, matters bearing upon the subject of the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) have been discussed, and the hon. member is to be commended for presenting it to the house. I am not going to enter into a discussion with all the medical gentlemen in this chamber on the question whether or not medicine should be nationalized, but we all recognize the splendid work the medical profession is doing all over the country. As I understand it, there is no intention on the part of the mover of the resolution to interfere in any way with the medical profession. His idea is that there should be some cooperation on the part of the Dominion government with the provincial authorities in health matters. I believe in such cooperation. I do not think the Dominion government should continue a healtn department that does not do anything to advance public health. So far as I can ascertain, the department as at present constituted does not justify its existence. The government must do one of two things: either give the department something to live for, or cut it off. So far as I am concerned I think the Dominion should take an interest in health matters.
I agree entirely with the remarks of the hon. member for Muskoka^Ontario (Mr. Mc-Gibbon) as to the splendid work which is being done by the Victorian Order of Nurses, the Red Cross Society, and other similar organizations. I have often thought it a shame that it should be necessary to appeal to the public for subscriptions for the purpose of looking after the health of the people of this country. In my constituency perhaps there is no necessity for anything of this kind, or possibly not to the extent that there is in other places, but I also have received many resolutions, particularly from women's organizations, advocating that something of this kind be done. I know that in the remote parts of British Columbia there is dire and urgent necessity for some provision whereby proper medical and nursing attention may be given.
I do not think it is sufficient for the government to say: We have not the money. The government seems to have the money when it wishes to spend any. The government is content to spend a lot of money here in Ottawa to tear down buildings and provide for a park which nobody seems to want, but when it comes to expenditure on public health, the excuse for inaction is that no money is available.

National Health-Mr. Dunning
I submit, sir, that the Minister of. National Health (Mr. King, Kootenay) should take this matter seriously. He is a man who undoubtedly knows perfectly well that the arguments he advanced this evening are entirely without foundation. As a medical man he must know he is simply beating the air. I believe he would like to see his department amount to something, but of course being a loyal supporter of his leader at all times he must do as he is told, and to-night when he said that really this was not a matter for the Dominion government, I think he was saying something that he himself did not believe.
The Minister of National Health is going to have many things to answer for when he goes to the country again, and this will be one of them. The speech that he made to-night is going to be used against him, and I warn him that it will have a very grave effect on the people of British Columbia and, I have no doubt, on the people of his own constituency who know him so well. I think -the government would be well advised to accept the resolution of the hon. member for Battle River and try to do something with its health department.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): Mr. Speaker, in spite of the implied threat in the words of the last speaker (Mr. McQuairrie) as to what will happen to anyone who speaks his mind on this subject, I think I had better discharge the duty which falls to a Minister of Finance in matters of this kind.
I have been impressed with the testimony which has come from all parts of the house to the splendid work now being carried on by the provinces and the municipalities in connection with public health. Every citizen of Canada feels proud of the tremendous advance which has been made in this country in public health matters during the last twenty years, and particularly during the last decade. That means, Mr. Speaker, that those public bodies which are at present constitutionally charged with responsibility for these matters are doing their duty, and doing it well.
The question before the house to-night is not whether such work shall be done; in fact we have eloquent testimony that it is being done to an increasing degree by those responsible for it. Rather the question is: Shall the Dominion step in, the constitution to the contrary notwithstanding, and enter upon Dominion expenditure in a field that hitherto has been provincial and municipal? Most of the arguments advanced for the Dominion entering this field of health units could be 
advanced with at least equal strength for the Dominion making payments towards hospitals in various parts of Canada. In fact the need for hospital accommodation in many parts of the Dominion is very much more acute in my opinion than the need for the organization of health units.

speechtext: Impossible.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
"Impossible," some hon. members say. Well, perhaps my hon. friends are not so familiar with conditions on the frontier as I am, and I can assure them that from the point of view of the women in a pioneer settlement, a hospital to go to in case of need, is very much more to be desired than some organization for the prevent tion of communicable diseases or for the other classes of work which are done by health units. Of .course, health units such as described by the mover of this resolution (Mr. Spencer) and by the Minister of Health (Mr. King, Kootenay) are excellent things. But that is not the question. The question is: Shall this Dominion contribute towards such work, or shall it not? The resolution, it is true, asks that the government take this into consideration. That is a perfectly proper request; the government should take into consideration any such matter. But it is my duty to point out some obvious facte in the constitution.
Reference has been made by more than one speaker to the expenditures by the federal government on the health of animals. True, a great deal of money is spent by the Dominion government on the health of animals, that subject being one which comes within the definite purview of the government of Canada. But may I point out that the expenditure so made all down the years is a very definite contribution by the Dominion government to the health of the citizens of Canada? The major part of the expenditure of this Dominion on the health of animals is directly for the purpose of preventing the communication of disease from animals to human beings; that is largely what the money is being spent for.

subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext: If that be so, why not extend the expenditure further?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
Exactly; that is the
point, just how far shall the Dominion go? There is no question regarding our constitutional duty to spend money with respect to matters connected with the health of animals. That is our field and the testimony of members speaking to-night is undoubtedly that Dominion governments from time to time have recognized their responsibility in that

National Health-Mr. Dunning
regard. May I point out something which occurred to me as I listened to the discussion this afternoon and to-night, namely, the change that, has apparently taken place in the attitude of the commons of Canada toward public expenditure; and it is true not only of the commons of Canada, but of the commons of Great Britain, I believe. The right of the commons to control expenditure was hard won, and perhaps for that very reason the premier function of the commons for many years became the controlling of the expenditures made by the crown,-limiting them, reducing them. In the last fifty years, however, a change has come over the scene, and both in Great Britain and in Canada the tendency of the commons has been to demand increased rather than restricted expenditure. In going over some material, not with respect to this situation especially but more particularly with regard to the resolutions now on the order paper which involve either an increased expenditure or a reduced revenue, I was interested in looking up the proceedings of the British House of Commons on questions of this kind, and I find that during the discussion in 1921, when a serious situation confronted the British House of Commons, Sir Austen Chamberlain-I quote now from the British Hansard-spoke as follows:
I speak now not as a prophet but as a recorder of the past. During the whole time in which I held office, and for as great a number of years preceding that, it has been the fact that parliament has not helped any government at any period within my recollection to reduce or restrict expenditure. I am not talking in a party sense, I am not taking in defence or excuse of any expenditure by the present government which may be criticized, whether rightly or wrongly, but I am stating what I believe is a fact, that the right honourable member for Paisley (Mr. Asquith) would accept as historically true at any period within his knowledge. Hitherto, no matter what government has been in power, for the last thirty or forty, or perhaps even fifty years, pressure on the government of the day has always been, spend, spend. The cry of the House of Commons has been the cry of the horse leech's daughters, "Give, give", and resistance has had to be found in the department, in the treasury, or in the government.
I presume that in the British House of Commons motions of this kind have for their object the undoubted good of the people. Of course, much good can be done with considerable sums of money along very many lines, and particularly in matters of public health. I listened with great admiration to the speech of my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Maloney) in this debate, and I have reason to appreciate, from my own experience in the provincial field, the tremendous value of the work which can be done in the matter of
public health. But to come back to what I started with, the question is not the value or otherwise of activities to promote public health. The question we are now asked to consider is whether the Dominion government should step out and become a financial partner with provinces and municipalities from coast to coast, apparently without any control of expenditure for what is admittedly a good purpose, but a purpose which up to the present time in the history of Canada, has been progressively well discharged by those provinces and municipalities. And so I say that from the point, of view of the financing of the country -I a,m speaking not of immediate financial requirements, but in the general sense-that while the government should take into consideration all such proposals as requested by the House of Commons, it is necessary that any government at any time should count the cost-not merely for to-day or to-morrow, but the commitment involved upon the whole country in loading upon the treasury a scheme of this kind; and should also take into consideration the fact that whether we like it or not we have a federal system of government which does definitely divide, or practically so, the responsibilities and obligations as between various taxing authorities. The question really comes to this, Mr. Speaker: this being admittedly a good purpose towards which to direct the expenditure of public money, what public body in the Dominion shall be charged with the responsibility of taxing the people to that end? Hitherto it has been regarded as good policy that the taxing authority in matters affecting public health shall be, in the main, the provinces, and the provinces in the exercise of their undoubted constitutional rights have transferred a part of their responsibility to municipalities; in many cases have arranged that municipalities shall be responsible for the maintenance of their local hospitals, aided in most instances by grants from the .provincial treasury on the basis of so much per patient per day. That responsibility, I say, has been well discharged, and the method of discharging it is being improved upon daily by the provinces and the municipalities.
The question for this house to consider is whether the Dominion should go further, bearing in mind, as I have already pointed out, that the major part of the expenditure on health of animals really has a bearing upon the health of the people themselves. Canada is now committed to a very extensive programme of scientific research. Will anyone say that the solution of problems in pure science will not in many respects contribute

National Health-Mr. Dunning
to the public health? It is generally recognized that the greatest advances have been made, as mentioned by my hon. friend from South Renfrew, by the work of research scientists, and this Dominion has embarked upon enlarged activities in that direction.
In conclusion, I simply desire to ask the sympathy of the house from the point of view of this Dominion as a taxing authority. It must tax to discharge the national obligations. No one ever proposed, Mr. Speaker, that the provinces should ibe asked to help the Dominion by way of contribution toward the expenditure involved in the carrying out of national undertakings. Someone pointed out during the course of the debate that the Dominion looks after those who are maimed and hurt in the carrying out of their national duty during the war, and argued from that that the Dominion should go further and deal with the whole civilian population as well. No Dominion government has yet asked the provinces to vote money in order to help the federal government carry out its national obligation toward those who suffered in their war service overseas, and such proposal would be regarded as absurd. Again the question arises, what taxing authority can properly levy the taxes necessary to discharge this obligation? Obviously it would be regarded as ridiculous for any other than the national taxing authority to levy taxes in order to meet war pension expenditures and the other commitments arising out of war. Down through the years the provincial and the municipal unit have been employed for many purposes in matters coming within their jurisdictions; and while the Dominion government will undoubtedly take into consideration the representations made by hon. members to-night on this subject, I think I have a right to place before the house the principles to which I have alluded.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
I have listened with much interest to the observations of the hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) with respect to the discussion that has taken place. Touching the necessity for the establishment of health units, nothing need be said; I think the case is complete almost before it is stated. The question as to how the cost of maintaining such units is to be borne is another matter altogether. We can agree with much that the Minister of Finance has said. But let us look at this matter as practical persons. All taxes, whether raised by the Dominion, provincial or municipal authorities, are imposed upon the people of Canada, and the people of Canada pay the whole of that taxation.

It has been the custom of parliament from time immemorial-the very foundation of this parliament-to grant subsidies to the provinces. The basis of the federal union is the grant of subsidies by parliament to the provinces. Those subsidies were, in some instances based upon arbitrary considerations, in others on population. As time has gone on the provinces have received larger and larger grants from the federal exchequer. Why? Because the provinces are limited to direct forms of taxation, and the Dominion may raise taxes by any method or form of taxation. Therefore it follows that taxes can be raised much more readily by the Dominion taxing power, which has recourse to many sources of revenue, than by the provinces. The customs taxes in this country last year amounted to over $200,000,000. Those customs taxes were paid by all the people of Canada, and the Dominion government had the power to appropriate that sum of money to any purpose it thought to be of national interest. Part of that money was appropriated for the payment of subsidies to the provinces. Part of it was appropriated for other purposes. Part of it was appropriated to a federal commission with power to expend money for the beautifying of the city of Ottawa. They do not raise taxes, but they have the supreme control over the expenditures of the sum of money granted to them. Other money is given to the battlefields commission at Quebec; they spend it, but they do not raise it. There are other commissions which receive grants from this Dominion and expend them as they please, or in accordance with the terms of their creation, and they do not raise the money by taxation. That is clear. These are national undertakings. There are large sums of money appropriated to various purposes that are expended by the bodies into whose hands the moneys are entrusted without regard to the fact that they may not raise them because they have no taxing power.
Now, let us ask ourselves what this resolution means. What is meant is that there shall be an appropriation by this parliament of a sum of money to be placed in the hands of the provincial authorities for national health purposes. Remember, it is national health, not provincial health. Keep this in mind: the province deals with the municipal situation, with smallpox and matters of that kind; the province deals with epidemics in the communities and in some cases with hospitalization. There is, however, a field in which the province may not, it seems to me, properly function, and that is the creation of national wealth by ensuring the health of the Canadian people. Some one has said, " A nation's

National Health-Mr. Bennett
health is a nation's wealth." We as a parliament are concerned in the health of the Canadian people as a whole. To the extent to which men are able to labour, free from disease, we have added to the national wealth; to the extent which citizens by studying preventive medicine obtain knowledge, from clinics and other methods, for which the nation might well pay, we have added to the national wealth of Canada.
Did you ever consider the sums of money that are lost in this country through illness in a single year? Would any appropriation that might be made by this parliament to the provinces equal one-haLf the money represented by the loss to this country in one year through illness and inability of Canadians to work? It is an amazing figure, if you can rely upon figures as being in the least sense accurate. Parliament is charged with the responsibility for making laws for the peace, order and good government of Canada. There are certain specified heads under which we legislate. The provincial legislatures are charged with the responsibility for making laws within their own limited areas. There are specific heads under which they legislate, and health is, undoubtedly, one of them. But no province can undertake to deal with the subject of health as a problem concerning the nation as a whole, and one affecting the creation of greater national wealth in the truest and broadest sense I have mentioned, unless they have a grant in aid from this parliament.
Fifty years ago Disraeli in the English House of Commons moved an amendment to one of Gladstone's budgets asking that money be appropriated from the Imperial exchequer to assist in the defraying of costs of local organizations in Great Britain. One of the largest appropriations of modern times was made by the British ministry only a few short months ago for the purpose of relieving industry from the burden of local taxation. Here we are asked to do what? We are asked merely to make a grant in aid of the effort which the provinces will carry forward to ensure the health of the Canadian people as a whole, not provineially but nationally, not in a narrow and circumscribed area but throughout this Dominion as a whole, in order that the knowledge of preventive medicine may become universal and in order that the greatest means known to man to increase the national wealth, namely, measures to ensure the national health of our people, may become an accomplished fact.
I am in support of this resolution for that reason. I believe it is absurd to say that this parliament is limited in the scope of its
powers or the exercise of its jurisdiction. This parliament may appropriate money for any purpose, and the parliament of Canada that can appropriate money for sufferers in the East or the West Indies or continental Europe when a great catastrophe happens surely can make an appropriation in aid of the provincial effort to ensure the health of the Canadian people. I say it is wrong for any Prime Minister to say it is a vicious principle that we should grant money to provinces because they do not raise it by taxation. It is no more a vicious principle to grant money to a province in order to ensure the health of the Canadian people, surely, than to grant money to a federal commission for the beautification of this city of Ottawa. Surely it cannot be so. Let us talk with some regard to reasonableness when we discuss the situation. I am fairly familiar with the commission which has been created for that purpose; I am acquainted with the grants which have been made and with other matters concerning it, but the fact is that this parliament makes grants to such commissions, and you cannot limit it by saying "this is within the legislative power of the province and this within the legislative power of the Dominion." We are dealing with a national problem, and the only way we can successfully deal with it is by making grants from the federal exchequer, in which is placed the money raised by different forms of taxation. We must make these grants to the provinces in order to enable them to carry on a work which otherwise they cannot properly undertake.
May I say this further word: During the last few years I have observed a constant and steady drying up of the sources of private benefaction. In the days of the war we all gave very freely, and then the provinces undertook larger responsibilities with respect to health. I recall that a Red Cross organization with which I was concerned maintained a hospital at Pouce Coupe, away in the frontier between British Columbia and Alberta. Today in Calgary we are maintaining, through the 'junior Red Cross, a hospital for crippled children, and the children in the schools are being taught the benefit of making contributions in aid of those weaker and less able to care for themselves. Every year as we pass the subscription list in an endeavour to secure funds we find that the people are being convinced that governments are undertaking the responsibility, with money obtained by taxation and which was formerly donated by private individuals. They will not pay twice; they will not be taxed on the one hand and give with the other. There is, I repeat, a constant drying up of the sources of revenue

National Health-Mr. Lapointe
from private benefactions and gifts, but there is no lessening of taxation. This country is not lessening taxation in volume. The question is what is to be done with the money, and I put it to the house and the country whether or not any better use could be made of a few million dollars than to grant to the provinces sufficient funds to enable them to maintain health units from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
The good will be reflected within a reasonable time. It has been reflected in England within the last ten years, and the statistics of one of the greatest insurance companies in the world indicate that by .pursuing these methods the span of human life has been extended nine years. That has been the result of twenty-five years experience. The Life Extension Institute, of which the former Chief Justice of the United States was chairman, provides for the examination every year of all who hold life insurance policies. This examination is given without cost and is for the purpose of extending the span of human life. Prevention is better than cure. Preventive medicine is the great study of to-day. I observe that a leading citizen of Great Britain, in delivering at the university of 'Leeds not long since an address upon preventive medicine, pointed out in language much better than I can employ the benefits to be derived from following such a course. Let us approach this .problem not as a problem of jurisdiction, not as a problem as to whether or not under the British North America Act it is a matter of provincial responsibility; let us look upon it as a national problem. This parliament has the power to appropriate any part of the national revenue for any purpose for the interest of Canada as a whole. Make the appropriation not for provincial purposes, but to the provinces to carry forward a great national undertaking- the ensuring of the health and thereby the happiness and prosperity of the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I desire at the outset
to say that I am going to vote in favour of this resolution, which merely asks that the government should take into consideration the advisability of making grants to the provinces equal to one-third the cost of establishing, and to cover permanently such full-time health units as may be organized.. However, I agree with the bon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MiacLaren) that the first step should co.me from the provinces, and when that step is made then the request should be considered. My object in rising is to state that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. 
Bennett) is not altogether fair to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) when he states that the power which raises taxation should be the one to spend the money raised by that means. He mentioned the federal district commission and the national battlefields commission as instances where federal money is spent by way of grants. Surely he knows that those two commissions are federal commissions.

speechtext: Surely.

speechtext:
They are appointed by
federal parliament and they are under the control of a responsible minister of the crown. Does the same thing apply in matters of health? When this parliament enacted the act to create the Department off Health, it specified by section 7:
Nothing in this act or in any regulations made hereunder shall authorize the minister or any officer of the department to exercise any jurisdiction or control over any provincial or municipal board of health or other health authority operating under the laws of any province.

subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext: That does not touch upon it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
Parliament knew that
there was a limitation of constitutional jurisdiction in matters of health as between the Dominion parliament and the provinces, and the whole act is framed with that condition in view. The act clearly states that nothing therein shall invade upon the provincial area as far as matters of health are concerned. It is a federal act and in no way are we authorized to trespass upon provincial control.
My hon.. friend is quite right in stating that the provinces are limited to direct taxation. They have been compelled to ask for increases in their subsidies, which they received, and further increases may be made; but a far better principle is that we should give subsidies to the provinces without earmarking them for any special purposes. The provinces are jealous of their autonomy, and I do not think that it is in the provincial interests that we should give them money for a certain purpose and exercise control which might limit their jurisdiction. The principle of making grants and earmarking them for special purposes provincial in scope is not a good principle and I for one would rather increase the subsidies to the provinces and leave them absolutely free to act within their jurisdiction.

subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say at the outset that I agree with the remarks and am very much in sympathy with the sentiments of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). I am jealous for

National Health-Mr. Young (Saskatoon)
the rights of the provinces and I do not believe in mixing these things up. The provinces, being autonomous, should conduct their own affairs. They are responsible for their own citizens and they should have complete freedom within their own boundaries. I have often thought that the Dominion parliament should, be in a sense, a confederation; that is, it should be exactly what the provinces make it. Under present conditions and circumstances, under the false fiscal policy which we are pursuing to-day, the provinces have reached the stage where they cannot meet their indebtedness; they cannot raise by taxation sufficient money to meet their obligations. As time has gone on it has become more and more necessary for the Dominion government to give assistance to the provinces for different purposes; I have in mind the road policy and the farm loan scheme. These things were brought into being by this parliament because the provinces themselves could not meet the needs of agriculture. To help the provinces as regards health is another matter of the same kind. In Saskatchewan to-day we are unable to meet our obligations regarding farm loans. It has become necessary for the government, under the present false fiscal policy, to subscribe more and more liberally as time goes on to the schemes of the provinces themselves. The little group in this corner, not so very long ago, had to stand the insult from an hon. member from Toronto who said that we were beating the income tax collector, and that Toronto itself paid thirty per cent of the income tax of the whole Dominion. That very statement is in itself a charge that the provinces are unable to meet their obligations, because the money has been concentrated in the hands of a few.
Health is one of the most important matters a province has to deal with, and when it cannot meet its obligations to its citizens, where shall it look but to where its taxes go? The Minister of Finance said that the provinces do not subscribe to the schemes of the Dominion for pensions and so on, but every individual is being taxed for that purpose. We are spending many millions of dollars on the beautification of this city. I want to ask whether the beautification of Ottawa, upon which these millions are being spent, is of more importance than the health of our people. The members from the maritime provinces very well know that they have been unable to carry on, and the western provinces to-day are as much in need of a Duncan commission as the maritime provinces ever were, simply on account of the concentration of wealth through a false fiscal policy
adopted by this parliament. The matter of looking after the health of our people is only one item among many. We are getting further every year along this wrong road of a wrong fiscal policy, and it is becoming more and more imperative that the Dominion government return some of its money to the provinces to look after the health and general welfare of the people.

speechtext:
It is not necessary for me to say
that I regard the health of the people of Canada as one of the most important matters, if not the most important, to which we can give attention. In fact it is not necessary to take up the time of the house in discussing the question. I say at once that I regard the health of the people of Canada as of paramount importance. I might also say that I regard the education of the people of this country as a matter of very great importance. I might go on to say that I regard good roads throughout Canada as of very great importance. I might also say that I regard having churches in every part of the country ns of great importance. Then I might ask the question: Since someone has to pay, who are the people who should pay for these various items? We are sitting here as members from constituencies, but we represent the whole of Canada. The peculiar thing about this resolution is that it comes from a member of the House of Commons. It seems to me that if the provinces feel that they are unable to deal with this vital problem, this is a resolution which might very properly be introduced by a member of any provincial legislature. Then, if all the legislatures throughout Canada were of a common mind in the conclusion that they could not properly discharge the function of adequately looking after the health of the people, they might ask the parliament of Canada to assist them in the discharge of that duty. But it does not seem to come in that particular way, and I therefore suggest that before parliament should feel obligated to deal with a matter of this kind, the least we .could expeict would be that the provinces themselves would make this request.
May I ask this question? If to-night, instead of the word "health," we substitute the word "education," and if the parliament of Canada made large grants to the provinces for education, at the same time would it not be fair to say that we would have some interest in the policy of education in each province? I would like to ask the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) whether his friends in Saskatchewan at this moment would like us to vote
23S
National Health-Mr. Esling

in the parliament of Canada money for educational purposes, and I would like to ask him at the same time whether he thinks his friends in, Saskatchewan would like this parliament to dictate the policy of education in the legislature of Saskatchewan. Every province in Canada is so jealous of its rights in that regard that it would have something to say in the matter. My view is that before giving money through the federal parliament for a matter of this kind we should at least expect the various provinces to make a request for it.
I am not sure that we could not very properly grant money for the purpose stated in the resolution. I feel so strongly on the health question that I would like to say this: if the provinces, on account of their more limited taxing powers, find themselves unable to discharge properly and adequately the function which any health department should discharge, I would be in favour of the federal parliament granting the money. But I cannot help feeling that the first request should come not from a member of the federal house but from the provincial legislatures themselves.

speechtext:
In so far as this resolution applies to British Columbia, may I state that we have local health units there, and the various institutes and other bodies which have made a request for a grant have asked simply that such grant be made as a substitute for the grant that now comes from the Rockefeller Foundation? In British Columbia the local units are provided for with one-half contribution from the local district, one-quarter from the province, and one-quarter from the Rockefeller Foundation. The Rockefeller grant runs temporarily for a period of three years, and it is to make good that grant after its expiration that the various bodies in British Columbia ask for federal assistance.
Communities which are near the larger centres of population are better able to take care of themselves, but if some of the members who are not familiar with the remote districts could understand the impossibility of furnishing medical assistance to families living away up in such far-off districts that it takes a doctor a week to get in and out, they would better appreciate the need of. a federal grant in this direction. As I say, we are able to take care of those units in the centres of population, but those in the more remote districts are practically without any medical attention, and I think the people of the institutes in British Columbia are fully

justified in asking the federal government to contribute merely that portion of the expense which is now covered by the Rockefeller grant, or, in other words, one-quarter of the existing expenses.

speechtext:
I think that to-day's discussion covering one point and another has afforded a splendid exemplification of the purpose and function of private members' day, giving as it does an opportunity to the various private members of the house to bring forward their suggestions and express their opinions on many important matters without reference to party lines or political feelings. I think too, Mr. Speaker, that perhaps no more important subject could1 have occupied the attention of the private members to-day than this very subject of national health. I think we are to 'be .congratulated1 upon the many expressions of opinion and the unanimity of feeling exhibited throughout this house on this question. There were, however, two or three points that occurred to me as the debate proceeded to which I should like to refer for a moment.
In the first place I would refer to the suggestion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) 'as to the provincial character of such undertakings as those 'bearing upon the subject matters of the resolution. To my mind we must consider the question very much as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has considered it, from the point of view that Whatever we do, whatever public expenditures are made, under whatever public authority, the same people have to pay the taxes. We should therefore consider under what authority or under what combination of authorities this work can be most efficiently and most thoroughly done. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is essential that the national government should taike some part in this work, for as I see it, just as no small community can successfully take care of the health of the people -because, passing as they do from one community to another, it is impossible for the small 'Community adequately to protect them -thus making it necessary for the province to step in and coordinate, and expand that work, enlarging the area within which the control is exercised; so, following exactly the same argument, must the federal government step in if the work is to be done thoroughly and carried on beyond the bounds of the province. It requires coordination throughout the whole Dominion. We know perfectly well that our own citizens and people entering Canada from other countries pass from one community to another and from one province

National Health-Mr. Speakman
to another carrying with them the seeds of infection and disease; in order therefore to ensure the health both of those who travel and of those who stay at home it is necessary that all should come under some system of supervision. It makes no difference in the long run as to the amount of money the people must pay-we are all agreed on that- and I believe that the work can be most effectively done by the federal government itself, expanding and coordinating it from coast to coast.
There is another point which has been mentioned and which I think will bear repetition, namely the intimate connection which must exist .between any policy of immigration and the health of the nation. That immigration policy, being purely under the direction of the federal government, to my mind carries with it the necessity of life preservation. Immigrants must be followed wherever they go; medical attention and medical examination must 'be available to them wherever they may be, they must feel that .careful preventive measures are accompanying them. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the time will come, and it is approaching, when all this work will be done through the cooperation of all the different public bodies that are equally interested in it.
There is one other thought that passed through my .mind as the debate continued. It was stated by the Minister of Finance that it was purely a question as to the taxing body which should provide the .funds; that it was not a question of work crying out to be done and .being neglected; that the work was being well done by the provinces and municipalities. So far as I have seen the work has been done to the extent that the provinces and the municipalities have 'been able to carry it on, but their efforts have 'been strictly limited by their inability to finance these enterprises to the extent that they would like. The same work would ibe better done and would be carried further, and the health of the people would be more adequately safeguarded, if this motion were not only given consideration, as I know it will be, but if its principle were ultimately accepted by this parliament and if the terms laid down by the motion were put into effect.

subtopic: PROPOSED GRANT TO PROVINCES IN AID OF FULL TIME HEALTH UNITS
speechtext:
This is a question, Mr. Speaker, that is of vital importance to all portions of Canada. The discussion, if it has done nothing else, has drawn the attention of all Canada to the condition that now exists. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of thi6 house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of making grants to the provinces equal to one-third the cost of establishing, and to cover permanently such full time health units as may be organized.
The responsibility of the different governments has been repeatedly- pointed out in this debate. For six or seven years I was very closely identified in the rural parts of Canada with a union municipal hospital, as chairman, of the management committee. The hospital was entirely under the jurisdiction of the municipal unit, and it worked very efficiently. I believe that more money should be spent on health, but I am inclined to agree' with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), that if the various provincial governments have not at their command sufficient moneys for the purpose larger grants might be made to the provinces to further this work.
There is another point. I think it is always a sound principle that the taxes should be spent by the body that has the responsibility of collecting them. If any group or any individual has the responsibility both of collecting and of spending money, I believe that expenditures will .be made more judiciously-. I realize that the work of the municipalities and of the provinces may be limited by the state of their finances, but I think that difficulty could be overcome if the provinces, as suggested by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young) should appeal for aid to the -federal government, and if this suggestion had come from them I think every member of this house would have been prepared to support the resolution. For my .part, while I am in sympathy with the object of the resolution, I think the suggestion has not come, as it should have come, from the provinces, and like the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Justice, until the provinces do suggest that we make larger grants to them, I do not feel that I can support the resolution.

I feel very well repaid Mr. Speaker, for introducing this resolution. We have had an excellent debate, and nearly twice as many members have taken part in it as spoke on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. What is more, on this subject they have all been in agreement as to the importance of the work to be done; the only difference was in the view held on the
National Health-Mr. Spencer

government side as to whether the expenditure should be made out of the federal treasury, and how it should be made.
It is not necessary for me to go over the speeches that have been made except to touch on one or two points, particularly those made by the Minister of Health (Mr. King, Kootenay). Onie of his statements should really disarm three or four members on his own side; he said that two provincial governments had already approached him, as Minister of Health, to help in this matter. That, I think, will answer the objections of the hon. member who last spoke (Mr. Vallance), the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MacLaren), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young). The Minister of Health stated that owing to the fact that the United States had gone so very largely into this system of organization for the care of public health they had made it possible to prevent great epidemics. One can easily see how that would result. He said this resolution was the natural demand of following the work achieved on the other side of the line, and that it should be dealt with by our public men. I am very glad to get his admission. However, he did what I was afraid he would do; he brought the old British North America Act to his defence and got behind it, saying that it would not allow the federal authorities to do this. I may refer the house to fourteen items in the current estimates running from $5,000 to $100,000 and representing grants by the government of Canada to this, that and the other thing. If the British North America Act does not prevent them from giving these grants, I am sure my suggestion would be in order.

I was referring to the
Minister of Health. The member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) referred to the way this system of organization would work in with the system we have, particularly in Alberta, of municipal hospitals. The member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) referred to the wonderful work such an organization could do in the prevention of goitre so prevalent in the district to which she referred.
In reply to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), I would say that he should look back to the program of his party made in 1919 as cited by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead). At that time the Liberal party stood foursquare for tihe very work I am suggesting now, blaming the government of the day for not doing it, and saying they would understake the work if they got into power. If promises are of any value, then I say let us see them carried out.
I think if a whole lot of money was cut out from the immigration estimates and placed in aid of the conservation of public health across this Dominion, such an expenditure would be an investment, and a very good investment indeed. That is all I ask for in this resolution. I do not ask for an unremunerative expenditure, I ask for an investment, and it would be one of the very best investments Canada ever made.
